deep.reconstruction:
Setting. The notes concern arrangements of pseudolines in a real projective plane X (with X~ presumably a covering, e.g. the 2-sphere or a frame bundle). The orange 'X' marks are crossings (vertices) of the arrangement. The brown numbered strands record the order in which the other pseudolines cross a moving element. The green and yellow arcs are two positions of a distinguished pseudoline D.

1. Torsor bookkeeping for a 'fuseau'. A fuseau is a digon or lune bounded by two arcs ('murs') joining two vertices ('extrémités'). Grothendieck attaches three 2-element sets, each a Z/2-torsor: a (the two walls), Γ (the two extremities) and Ω (the two orientations of the fuseau). He records the identification Ω ≃ a ∧ Γ (contracted product of Z/2-torsors). He then relates Ω, after twisting by Γ (Ω' ≃ Ω ∧ Γ ≃ a ∧ Ω''), to the torsor of local orientations of X at a vertex of the fuseau. Once a wall D ∈ a is chosen, a is trivialised (a ≃ {±1}), and Ω becomes identified with the orientations ω of D. The NB identifies a fuseau with a critical relative position ('p.r. critique') together with a chosen vertex on it, which he calls an 'élément de contact'.

2. Pivoting circuit. Start from a sub-stable position D through a vertex s ∈ S_D (light green in the figure). Choose a rive ρ, i.e. a local side or generalisation of D at s, and an orientation ϖ of D; ϖ fixes the order in which triangles are swept. Equivalently, given ρ, one may choose an orientation ϖ of X at s. Rotating D about s then produces a cyclic sequence of stable relative positions D_1, …, D_8, D_9 = D_1. Consecutive positions differ by passing D across one vertex of the arrangement, i.e. a triangle flip. The small circle diagram, with radial D_0 … D_5 around a centre, is the pencil picture of this rotation.

3. Equivalence of data. Giving (D, ϖ, ω) is the same, up to sign, as giving the fuseau D defines plus an orientation of X at its vertex plus a choice of 'deployed' vertex.

4. Inverse circuit and the action of σ_2. The inverse circuit D_2, D_1 = D_9, D_8, …, D_3, D_2 is obtained by changing both ρ and ω simultaneously. Hence the operation σ_2 on frames ('repères') of X~ corresponds to fixing ϖ (the orientation of X at s) while reversing the orientation of D, or equivalently the orientation of the fuseau.

The page thus sets up a sign-coherent parametrisation of the 'rotation of a pseudoline around a point' circuits. These are the combinatorial analogue of rotating a line through a point and recording successive permutations. It also expresses the reversal and orientation symmetries as a Z/2 × Z/2-type action on frames.
errors: No outright error is visible. The torsor identifications are stated without proof, and the line 'Ω' ≃ Ω∧Γ ≃ a∧Ω''' is ambiguous: which torsor is the local orientation of X at the vertex is not made explicit.
'Donner (D, ϖ, ω) revient au ± que…' is only an equivalence up to sign or choice. The precise bijection (which vertex, which side ρ) is left implicit.
The figure labels (numbered strands 1–8, '1=5', 'ε=1', '5/6', '1/2') are not tied to the text, so the exact count of the circuit (8 positions) cannot be fully checked from this page.

ideas.what: Encoding the combinatorial symmetries of a lune/digon (walls, ends, orientations) as Z/2-torsors with contracted-product relations Ω ≃ a ∧ Γ
ideas.modern_name: Torsor/orientation-sheaf bookkeeping (contracted products of μ_2-torsors) applied to cells of a pseudoline arrangement
ideas.usually_credited_to: General technique; Grothendieck's own style (orientation torsors)
ideas.where_published: Torsor formalism appears throughout SGA; its application to pseudolines is unpublished as far as known

ideas.what: Circuit of stable positions obtained by rotating a pseudoline D about a vertex s, passing successively through critical positions (triangle flips)
ideas.modern_name: Allowable sequences / circular sequences of permutations; pencils through a point and single-element extensions of rank-3 oriented matroids; triangle (Ringel) flips
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goodman–Pollack (allowable sequences, ~1980–84); Ringel (1956, flips); Levi (enlargement lemma)

ideas.what: Fuseau identified with a critical relative position plus a chosen vertex ('élément de contact')
ideas.modern_name: Codimension-one stratum (degenerate/critical configuration) in the space of pseudoline positions; walls of a chamber structure
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in mutation-graph / realisation-space literature (Ringel, Goodman–Pollack, Björner–Las Vergnas–et al.)

ideas.what: Reversal of the circuit equals simultaneous change of rive ρ and orientation ω; the operation σ_2 on frames of X~ fixes the local orientation at s and flips the orientation of D
ideas.modern_name: Action of a small symmetry group (Klein-type) on flags/frames compatible with the rotation circuit; reversal symmetry of allowable sequences
ideas.usually_credited_to: Reversal symmetry of circular sequences is standard (Goodman–Pollack)

missed.claim: Independently of Goodman–Pollack, Grothendieck is building the 'rotating pseudoline around a point' circuit, i.e. an allowable-sequence-type object. He organises its orientation ambiguities via torsors and an action (σ_i) on frames of a cover X~. That is a groupoid/torsor formulation of the symmetries of circular sequences, which is not the standard presentation in oriented matroid theory.
missed.quote: Ainsi, l'opération σ_2 sur les repères de X~ correspond à l'opération qui fixe ϖ (orientation en S) et qui change l'orientation de D
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a modest piece of historical evidence that Grothendieck's 1983–84 pseudoline programme reached sweeping/pencil structures. A frame-bundle and torsor viewpoint on the space of pseudoline configurations could interest people studying realisation spaces and the topology of spaces of arrangements. Its mathematical content is likely subsumed by known theory.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is a careful, Grothendieck-flavoured sign and orientation bookkeeping for the known operation of rotating a pseudoline about a point through triangle flips. That is close to Goodman–Pollack allowable sequences and contemporaneous with them. It is interesting as history of his little-known pseudoline project, but there is no apparent new theorem.
transcription_corrections: The first-line markers transcribed '1°' and '2°' are, in the image, the torsor letters 'a' (the two walls) and 'Γ' (the two extremities). This is consistent with the boxed relation 'Ω ≃ a ∧ Γ'.
The parenthetical at top right reads approximately '(= côtés des fuseaux)' attached to 'des deux murs'.
'Ω ≃ σ ≃ ω' should probably read 'Ω ≃ ω' (set of orientations of D); the middle symbol is uncertain.
The figure labels near the vertices of the lower figure ('1=5', 'ε=1', '5/6', '1/2') are uncertain and may read 'ε=5', 'ε=1', 's/6', 'a/2'.
The final words 'une des contrebandes [?]' are illegible in part. The sense is 'a sommet (déployé) of the fuseau', i.e. a choice of one of its ends.
